ch02.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路), today Fuzhou Road, was a street of the International Settlement famous for its bookshops, teahouses, theaters and newspaper offices, and notorious for its brothels. The produce market of these opening scenes was a real building at the Fuzhou–Zhejiang Road corner, completed in 1930 and among the most modern in the city; the library on its upper floors, with the disused room behind the stacks, is where the meeting is laid. (Corroborated.)

The Zhejiang Grand Theater (浙江大戏院), on Zhejiang Road directly facing the market, was a real Art Deco cinema of 1930 — the first Shanghai theater by the Hungarian architect László Hudec (邬达克), whose buildings recur through these chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) governed the foreign-run International Settlement, and its own force, the Municipal Police, policed it. Because the Nationalists' Longhua garrison had no lawful power to make arrests inside the Settlement, it had to work through the Council's police; that jurisdictional seam runs through the whole of the arrest. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: The amusement ground had a forlorn look
ch02.note: The World Hotel (世界大旅社), with its roof-garden amusement ground overlooking the market, is one of the story's Shanghai settings; rooftop pleasure gardens of this kind were a real feature of the Fourth Avenue district, though the sources consulted differ on whether this particular hotel is documented. It is not the famous Great World (大世界) amusement arcade. (Uncorroborated.)

The Lyceum Theatre (兰心大戏院), the Settlement's principal Western theater and home of its British amateur dramatic society, is given here by its standing English name; the building of these years, opened in 1931, still stands on today's Maoming Road South. (Corroborated.)

Cuckoo Soul Abroad (海外鹃魂) was an early 1930s film of the Lianhua company; its star Jin Yan (金焰), a Korea-born actor hailed as the 'Emperor of Film,' played opposite the actress Ziluolan. In classical verse the cuckoo (杜鹃) is said to weep blood for grief, which sharpens Wei Dafu's joke that all three leads end up dead. (Jin Yan and the Lianhua title are corroborated; the film's exact cast is not.)

Longhua (龙华), southwest of the city, was the seat of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command and its prison, beside the Longhua Temple and its ancient pagoda. In February 1931 the Nationalists secretly shot some two dozen Communists here—the 'Longhua Martyrs,' among them the 'Five Martyrs' of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, Yin Fu, Feng Keng and Li Weisen), a killing mourned by Lu Xun. It is to this garrison that the prisoners of the novel are taken. (Corroborated.)

The Generalissimo (委员长) is Chiang Kai-shek (蒋介石, 1887–1975), chairman of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission and head of the KMT government and army. In the winter of 1932–33, the novel's moment, he was directing the Fourth Encirclement Campaign against the Communists' Central Soviet. (Corroborated.)

Mount Lu (庐山, Lushan), above Jiujiang in Jiangxi, was the Nationalist government's summer seat, where Chiang Kai-shek kept a villa and transacted business of state; a petitioner such as Du Yuesheng seeking the Generalissimo's ear would indeed go up the mountain. (Corroborated.)

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (招商局), founded by the Qing statesman Li Hongzhang (here 'Grand Secretary Li'), was at the center of a real 1933 scandal. Li's grandson Li Guojie (李国杰), who ran one of its arms, was accused of mortgaging the company's Shanghai wharves—among them the Jinliyuan of the earlier scene—for a vast loan and pocketing the kickback, with Chen Fumu (陈孚木) as a go-between; a Shanghai court sentenced Li to eight years in April 1933. The gangster Du Yuesheng (the 'tycoon Du') hovers behind the affair as the detectives gossip it. (Corroborated; Du's exact role is not settled by the sources.)

ch03.note: The Central Party Affairs Investigation Section (党务调查科) was the Kuomintang's political-intelligence organ, run under the Central Organization Department by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique' and from 1929 by Xu Enzeng; those in the know called its Nanjing base, in the Zhanyuan garden, the 'Special Operations Headquarters.' It was the forerunner of the wartime Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (中统). You Tianxiao's secret post in it, outranking his open one, is the source of his double-dealing. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army
ch03.note: A 32nd Army of the National Revolutionary Army did exist, but it was Shang Zhen's (商震) Shanxi–Suiyuan force, stationed in Hebei in 1931–33, not at Shanghai; the units that actually held Longhua under the Songhu Garrison Command were others. Posting a '32nd Army' to the Shanghai garrison is the novel's own detail, not the historical record. (Contradicted.)

The pagoda beside the garrison is the ancient Longhua Pagoda, standardly 龙华塔; Bao'en Pagoda (报恩塔, 'Pagoda of Requited Kindness') is a genuine traditional alternate name for it, from the legend that Sun Quan of Wu raised it to repay his mother. The source thus uses a historically valid variant, not a mistake. (Corroborated.)

Xi Shi (西施), a legendary beauty of the state of Yue in the Spring and Autumn era, was by tradition sent to beguile the king of rival Wu and hasten its ruin—the archetypal planted agent. As a cryptonym for a mole inside the enemy's ranks it is pointed; the identity of 'Xi Shi' is one of the book's central secrets.

ch04.anchor: Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic
ch04.note: The Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic (危害民国紧急治罪法), promulgated by the Nationalist government on 31 January 1931, prescribed death for a range of acts against the state and was the chief legal instrument used against Communists; hence the interrogator's threat of the firing squad. (Corroborated.)

Haohan (浩瀚, 'the vast') is the working alias of a senior Communist the enemy is hunting; within the Party he was known for articles published under the name in The Guide Weekly (向导), the Central Committee's organ of the 1920s. His whereabouts, and who among the arrested may be his contact, are the engine of the plot.

Winter (冬) is Ling Wen's own novel, a book within the book; like Ling Wen and the other principals it is the author's invention. The novel's protagonists are fictional, set against a real historical background; its closing appendix frames the whole as an homage to the real, largely nameless Communists executed at Longhua. (The title Winter echoes the name of Ling Wen's late husband, Long Dong, 龙冬.)

The May Thirtieth Movement (五卅运动) was the wave of anti-imperialist strikes and protests that swept China after Settlement police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai on 30 May 1925; it drew many, like Ling Wen and her husband, into the revolution. The Northern Expedition she goes on to mention set out from Guangzhou in 1926; the Nationalist purge of Communists began in 1927. (Corroborated.)

Tanhuang (滩簧) opera is a family of Jiangnan folk sung-drama forms in the Wu dialect, out of which grew Shanghai opera (沪剧) and its Suzhou and Wuxi cousins; the comparison casts Miss Tao's laughter as broad and theatrical. (Corroborated.)

ch05.note: Da Hong Pao (大红袍, 'Great Red Robe') is the most storied of the Wuyi 'rock teas,' a heavily oxidized oolong grown on the cliffs of Mount Wuyi in Fujian and long counted among the most prized teas in China.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) was the Cantonese force that put up fierce resistance to the Japanese at Shanghai in the 'January 28' Incident of 1932 (一·二八, the first Battle of Shanghai); it was afterwards sent to fight Communists in Fujian. 'Commander Cai' is the army's general Cai Tingkai (蔡廷锴). (Corroborated.)

Xuanwu Lake (玄武湖) lies against the northeastern wall of Nanjing; the drive in this chapter runs beside its stretch of the great Ming-dynasty city wall, past Jiming Temple (鸡鸣寺) and out by the Shence Gate (神策门). Nanjing was the Nationalist capital and the seat of the secret-service headquarters to which You Tianxiao reports.

ch06.note: The encirclement and suppression campaigns (围剿) were the Nationalists' successive military drives from 1930 against the Communist base areas, above all the Central Soviet (中央苏区) in Jiangxi–Fujian, whose capital was Ruijin; the Communists fought them as 'counter-encirclement.' The Fourth was under way in the winter of 1932–33. In the movement's usual geography the country divided into 'Red' or Soviet areas and the 'White areas' (白区) under Nationalist rule, where the novel's underground works. (Corroborated.)

Brigade Commander Weng is Weng Zhaoyuan (翁照垣, 1892–1972), a brigade commander of the Nineteenth Route Army who took the first Japanese assault at Zhabei on the night of 28 January 1932; both the man and the Zhabei defense are historical. He is a different man from the Cantonese 'Adjutant Weng' of the earlier chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Guangzhou Uprising (广州起义, the Canton Uprising of 11–13 December 1927) was a Communist insurrection that briefly proclaimed a 'Guangzhou Commune' before being crushed with heavy loss of life — the last of the failed urban risings of 1927. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: There are no miracles in nature or history
ch06.note: The lines Chen Qianyuan is translating are the opening of Lenin's Letters from Afar (远方来信), First Letter, written from Zurich in March 1917; the wording here follows the standard English of Lenin's Collected Works. The next chapter of the novel takes its title, 'A Letter from Afar,' from this same work. (Corroborated.)

ch07.note: In early 1933 Chiang Kai-shek directed the anti-Communist campaigns in person from Nanchang (南昌), Jiangxi; his formal Nanchang Field Headquarters (南昌行营) followed in May 1933, the forward command post for the Fourth and Fifth Encirclement Campaigns. (Corroborated.)

Xinjing (新京, 'New Capital,' today Changchun) was the capital of Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan proclaimed in the occupied Northeast in March 1932. A merchant 'from Xinjing' in 1933 Shanghai is thus a man arriving from Japanese-held Manchuria — a loaded provenance, and part of Chen Qianli's cover. (Corroborated.)

Shanhaiguan (山海关), the pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, was stormed and taken by Japanese forces on 1–3 January 1933, opening the Defense of the Great Wall campaign (长城抗战) as Japan pushed south from Manchuria; it fixes the novel's atmosphere of national crisis. (Corroborated.)
Shen Bao (申报), founded in 1872 and published in Shanghai, was the most important Chinese-language newspaper of the Republican era. (Corroborated.)

Khabarovsk (伯力), in the Soviet Far East, places Chen Qianli's three years of training in the USSR — the Soviet and Comintern schooling that stood behind many senior Chinese Communist operatives of the period; his long way out (Khabarovsk to Vladivostok, then by sea) follows a real clandestine route. The school itself is the novel's; the geography is real.

The Outpost (前哨) was the organ of the League of Left-Wing Writers; its first issue (April 1931), edited by Lu Xun (鲁迅) and Feng Xuefeng (冯雪峰), was a memorial number for the writers murdered at Longhua weeks before. This stretch of North Sichuan Road (北四川路) in Hongkou was the heart of the leftist literary world; Chen Geng (陈赓), the Red Army commander named here, really did meet Lu Xun secretly in Shanghai in 1932. (Corroborated.)

The Yihong Garden (扆虹园), a Cantonese garden-mansion in the North Sichuan Road quarter, was visited more than once by Sun Yat-sen (孙中山, 'Mr. Sun') — in 1912–13 Guangdong native-place associations fêted him there. (Corroborated.)

The Left League is the League of Left-Wing Writers (左联), founded in Shanghai in 1930; five of its young members were among the Communists shot at Longhua in February 1931 whom the novel commemorates. (Corroborated.)
The Nanchang Uprising (南昌起义) of 1 August 1927 was the Communists' first armed revolt against the Nationalists, afterwards marked as the founding day of the Red Army. (Corroborated.)

The German Hospital (德国医院) was the real Paulun Hospital (宝隆医院), founded in 1900 by the German physician Erich Paulun and tied to what became Tongji University's medical school; it stood in the Settlement, and its later descendant is Shanghai's Changzheng Hospital. (Corroborated.)

A surety bond (铺保, pubao) was a real institution of Republican Shanghai: a shop, pledging its name and chop, stood as guarantor for a third party — a tenant, an employee, or a prisoner seeking bail — and bore joint liability if that party defaulted. Here the underground turns the custom to its own use, springing arrested comrades on a shopkeeper’s guarantee. (Corroborated.)

ch08.note: The Grand Theatre (大光明大戏院), on today's West Nanjing Road, was Shanghai's most celebrated cinema; the László Hudec rebuild that made it an Art Deco landmark was completed in mid-1933, just as this chapter is set. (Corroborated.)

Marlene Dietrich (玛琳·黛德丽, 1901–1992), the German-American film star, had lately played 'Shanghai Lily' in Shanghai Express (1932); her face on a Shanghai cinema hoarding in 1933 is exactly of its moment. (Corroborated.)

Turandot, Puccini's last opera (premiered posthumously in 1926), is set in a legendary Peking whose princess beheads the suitors who fail her riddles; the poster's line condenses the opera's blood-soaked opening — the executioner's chorus, 'Gira la cote' ('turn the grindstone') — rather than quoting it. The touring San Carlo company was real, though a 1933 Carlton staging is not separately documented. (The opera corroborated; the Shanghai performance uncorroborated.)

As the Japanese advanced in early 1933, the Palace Museum in Beiping (北平, as Beijing was then called) began evacuating its treasures south; the first crates left the Forbidden City on the night of 5–6 February 1933, and the removal filled the newspapers exactly as the chapter describes. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Banks' Savings Society building
ch08.note: The tower going up across from the racecourse is the Park Hotel (国际饭店), developed by the Joint Savings Society of four banks (四行储蓄会) to a design by László Hudec and completed in 1934; at twenty-two storeys it was the tallest building in Asia for nearly thirty years. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: the Four Masters of the Ming
ch08.note: The Four Masters of the Ming (明四家) are Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming, Tang Yin and Qiu Ying (仇英); Qiu Ying alone was a professional artisan-painter, a master of meticulous brushwork whose much-prized manner made him one of the most heavily forged names in Chinese painting — apt for a tale of a fake. (Corroborated.)
The racecourse is the great oval of the Shanghai Race Club, a center of foreign social life; its grounds are today People's Square and People's Park. (Corroborated.)
The Grand Champagne (大香槟) was the Race Club's celebrated sweepstakes lottery, drawn on the big races; here the split ticket serves the plot as a recognition token. (Corroborated.)
The Xiaolin Guangji (笑林广记, 'Expanded Forest of Laughter') is the best-known of the classical Chinese joke-books, compiled in the Qing dynasty. (Corroborated.)

Morriss (马立斯) renders the name of the British Morriss family, proprietors of the North-China Daily News; the transliteration is well attested in old Shanghai, though the particular building named here, by the racecourse, is not separately documented. (The name corroborated; the building uncorroborated.)

ch09.note: The April Twelfth massacre (四一二, 1927) was Chiang Kai-shek’s sudden purge of his Communist allies in Shanghai on 12 April 1927, carried out with Green Gang gunmen against the workers’ pickets and unions. It shattered the first Nationalist–Communist united front and drove the Party into the deep-cover underground this novel depicts; casualty counts vary, and the wider ‘White Terror’ toll is estimated in the thousands and beyond. (Corroborated; exact figures are estimates.)

Wu Sibao (吴四宝) is the name of a real Shanghai figure (c. 1904–1942): a racecourse groom who became a chauffeur, rose through the Green Gang, and under the Japanese occupation led the armed unit of the collaborationist ‘No. 76’ secret service. The novel plants him here as a minor tenant, his groom-to-driver rise matching the record; that he was Ling Wen’s neighbor is the novel’s own touch. (The man corroborated; his role here the novel’s invention.)

ch09.anchor: A rabbit doesn't eat the grass by its own burrow
ch09.note: A Chinese proverb, 兔子不吃窝边草 — literally ‘a rabbit does not eat the grass beside its own burrow’ — meaning a rogue spares those closest to home. The point is that the racecourse tough keeps on civil terms with his own neighbors. (Idiom.)

A second landlord (二房东) is a sub-lessor who leases a whole house and lets its rooms on at a profit — a stock figure of crowded Shanghai. It is Ling Wen’s cover: the tenancy, taken in her late husband’s name, both houses her and, because a lease could not be revoked without cause, cannot easily be taken from her.

ch09.anchor: we've paid a bitter price for that before
ch09.note: The ‘bitter price’ alludes to the Party’s own real purges of 1930–31: the hunt for a supposed Nationalist network, the ‘AB Corps’ (AB团), and the Futian Incident of December 1930, in which thousands of Red Army personnel were arrested on coerced evidence and hundreds executed — a catastrophe Mao himself later acknowledged as a mistake. Yi Junnian’s caution against branding comrades as moles has this history behind it. (Corroborated; death tolls are estimates.)

Hongkou Park (虹口公园) was the largest public park of foreign Shanghai, in the Hongkou district; today it is Lu Xun Park (鲁迅公园). It was a real, popular place to stroll and be photographed — and, less than a year before this scene, the site of the 29 April 1932 bombing by the Korean patriot Yun Bong-gil. (Corroborated.)

The song is Tumbalalaika, a traditional Yiddish folk love-song of riddles, its refrain playing on the name of the balalaika, the Russian triangular-bodied lute the busker holds. Both song and instrument are real; the tune has nineteenth-century Eastern-European folk roots, and an Ashkenazi (Russian-Jewish) busker in 1930s Shanghai is historically plausible, that community predating the later refugee wave. (Corroborated.)

The Leica, made by Ernst Leitz of Wetzlar, was the pioneering 35mm miniature camera; the rangefinder Leica II appeared in 1932, so a Leica is exactly of this moment as a prestige, cutting-edge instrument. (Corroborated.)

ch10.note: The Zhonghui Bank (中汇银行), rendered here as the ‘Zhonghui Trust Bank,’ was real: founded in 1929 by the Green Gang boss Du Yuesheng, it ran a genuine trust department and safe-deposit vault, so a rented box there is authentic to the setting. (Corroborated; the ‘Trust Bank’ name follows the novel’s 信托银行.)

Guanshengyuan (冠生园) was a famous Shanghai food-and-confectionery company, founded in 1915 by Xian Guansheng and celebrated for its pastries and mooncakes; a well-known brand by 1933, its pastry box completes Ling Wen’s wealthy-wife disguise. (Corroborated.)

Here the source drops into stiff classical business-letter Chinese — 径启者 (‘I beg to state’), 大鉴, 为荷 — a formulaic epistolary register quite unlike the surrounding prose. The translation keeps that starched formality to mark the shift; the letter itself is a coded notice about a safe-deposit box.
The Rentai Bank Company (仁泰银公司), Lin Shi’s cover employer, is a realistic native-bank name but is not attested in the record and appears to be the novel’s invention. (Uncorroborated.)

Cut off from their leadership, the freed comrades form a provisional Party branch (临时党支部), improvising the Party’s cell structure so as to keep discipline and act together. It is also what licenses their alarming, self-appointed interrogation of Lin Shi.

ch11.anchor: A muddy Winter Solstice, a clear New Year
ch11.note: A Jiangnan weather proverb, 邋遢冬至清爽年: overcast, muddy weather at the Winter Solstice is taken to foretell a fine, clear New Year (and the reverse). It is folk lore, not meteorology. (Corroborated as a traditional saying.)

Jing’an Temple (静安寺), the ancient Buddhist temple on Bubbling Well Road (today Nanjing West Road), gave its name to the surrounding district. The custom of vying to burn the ‘first incense’ (头香) at the New Year, mentioned just below, is a real and famous feature of the place. (Corroborated.)

‘Cement’ here renders 水门汀, the Shanghainese transliteration of the English word (concrete); a 水门汀 house is a cement or reinforced-concrete building, the modern, desirable sort in 1930s Shanghai. (Corroborated.)
Zhaojiabang (肇嘉浜) was a real Shanghai creek, its banks crowded with wharves and yards in the 1930s; it was filled in during 1954–56 to make Zhaojiabang Road. (Corroborated.)

Massenet Road (马斯南路), the recognition-signal address, was a real French Concession street named for the composer Jules Massenet; today it is Sinan Road (思南路), the modern name chosen partly to echo the old one in Shanghainese. (Corroborated.)

The streets Wei Dafu reels off are all real roads of the old western Concessions: Haige Road (海格路, Avenue Haig; today Huashan Road), Shanzhong Road (善钟路, the one Concession road named for a Chinese, the land magnate Tao Shanzhong; today Changshu Road), and Zhaozhujiao Road (赵主教路, Route Monseigneur Maresca, for the Catholic bishop of Nanjing; today Wuyuan Road). (Corroborated.)

Red China (红色中华) was the real newspaper of the Chinese Soviet Republic’s central government, first published at Ruijin on 11 December 1931; the Third Counter-Encirclement Campaign whose victory it reports was the Red Army’s defeat, in the autumn of 1931, of the Nationalists’ third ‘encirclement and suppression’ drive against the Central Soviet. To keep a copy in the White area was dangerous in itself. (Corroborated.)
An Old Bolshevik is a veteran who joined the Party in its earliest years; applied to Old Yi, it marks his seniority and long standing in the revolution.

The Tiangu Estate (田谷邨) is a new-style lane compound on the real, exclusive Yuyuan Road; the specific name is not attested (it echoes the actual 愚谷邨, Yugu Cun, on that street), though the setting and building type are true to the period. (The street corroborated; this estate uncorroborated.)

ch12.note: Tilanqiao Prison (提篮桥监狱), the ‘Ward Road Gaol,’ was built by the International Settlement authorities in Hongkou and opened in 1903; long one of the largest prisons in the Far East — it was nicknamed ‘the Far East’s No. 1 prison’ — it still stands. Chen Qianli passes its gate in the foreign-flavored streets north of Suzhou Creek. (Corroborated.)

By the early 1930s the lanes of Hongkou around Tilanqiao were already a foreign working-class quarter — Russian émigrés who had fled the 1917 Revolution, and Russian and Baghdadi Jews among others — with institutions such as the Ohel Moshe Synagogue (its building of 1927) nearby. This earlier settlement predates, and is distinct from, the crowded refugee ‘ghetto’ the Japanese would impose on the same district in 1943 for Jews who fled Nazi Europe after 1938; the old man in the orange skullcap belongs to the older layer. (Corroborated.)

The tingzijian (亭子间) is the small, cheap back room over the kitchen landing of a Shanghai lane house — north-facing, low and cramped, the least desirable room to let, and so the classic lodging of the poor left-wing writers of 1930s Shanghai, the ‘tingzijian writers’ (亭子间文人). (Corroborated.)

Ye Tao (叶桃), here named for the first time, is Ye Qinian’s daughter and Chen Qianli’s love; her death — which Chen lays at her father’s door, and which the enemy means to fasten on Chen — is the buried wound that drives him, and, on the other side, feeds Ye Qinian’s hatred. Like the novel’s other principals she is the author’s invention. (Fiction.)

Nekrasov is the Russian poet Nikolai Nekrasov (1821–1877). The line the brothers keep as a private countersign — ‘They say the storm is coming, and I cannot help but smile’ — adapts a couplet from his early poem The Storm (Burya); but that poem is a light love lyric, not a political one — a young man, after a thunderstorm spoils a garden tryst, ever after smiles rather than frowns to hear a storm coming. The novel re-weaponizes its storm-and-smile image, and the Chinese ‘they say…is coming’ freely paraphrases the original. (The poem and the line are corroborated; the revolutionary coloring is the novel’s.)

Shaoshan (少山) was a real cover name of Zhou Enlai (周恩来) in the Shanghai underground — the name under which, in the 1932 ‘Wu Hao Incident,’ a lawyer publicly rebutted a forged notice of his defection. Sending Chen Qianli to the USSR through ‘Comrade Shaoshan’ borrows the historical alias; strictly, Zhou had already left Shanghai for the Central Soviet by late 1931, so the handler of this early-1933 scene is a compressed, literary use of the name. (The alias is corroborated as Zhou’s; the scene is the novel’s.)

Duoyunxuan (朵云轩), founded in Shanghai in 1900, was a celebrated studio for fine paper, fans and painting supplies, famous for decorated letter-paper printed by woodblock watermark. That the poem is written on a sheet printed with a spray of peach blossom is a private stroke: 桃, táo, ‘peach,’ is the given name of Ye Tao (叶桃). (The studio is corroborated; the peach-blossom pun is the novel’s.)

The Esperanto study group and Teacher Ye’s dictum that ‘the world of the future will have but one language’ place him in a real milieu: Chinese anarchists were among the earliest champions of Esperanto, which they promoted as a coming universal tongue that would dissolve nation and state. Ye Qinian’s early anarchism, and his scorn for ‘those Russian books,’ belong to that world. (Corroborated.)

ch12.anchor: the rice-water for the secret writing
ch12.note: The rice-water (米浆水) is invisible ink: a message written in rice-starch water dries unseen and is brought out by brushing the paper with tincture of iodine, which turns the starch strokes blue-black. Cheap and untraceable, it was a genuine and much-used method of the Communist underground’s clandestine correspondence. (Corroborated.)

ch13.anchor: the Eve of the Abolished Calendar
ch13.note: From 1929 the Nanjing government pressed the ‘National Calendar’ (国历, the Gregorian) on the country and set out to abolish the lunar year, banning its holiday, its New Year calls and its firecrackers; the old calendar was officially styled the ‘abolished calendar’ (废历), so that lunar New Year’s Eve became the Eve of the Abolished Calendar. As the chapter shows, the public almost wholly ignored the ban and kept the old year as before. (Corroborated.)

The Cathay Hotel (华懋饭店), Victor Sassoon’s Art Deco landmark on the Bund (part of Sassoon House, opened 1929, today the north building of the Peace Hotel), gives the chapter its title and its stage: the green pyramidal roof, the octagonal lobby rotunda under its colored-glass dome, and the revolving door at the Bund entrance are all real. Ye Qinian’s choosing to lodge ‘in Sassoon’s own house, in the house of the imperialists’ is pointed. (Corroborated.)

The sneezing foreigner in the star-patterned sweater is George Bernard Shaw. On his round-the-world cruise Shaw reached Shanghai on 17 February 1933, where in a few hours he met Soong Ching-ling, Cai Yuanpei and Lu Xun; days before, at the University of Hong Kong (11–12 February), he had scandalized the colonial authorities by urging the students to revolution — ‘if you are not a red revolutionist at twenty…’ The mobbing reporters and the world cruise are real; the sneeze and the sweater are the novel’s color. (Corroborated.)
The seventy-two transformations are the shape-shifting powers of the Monkey King, Sun Wukong, in the classic novel Journey to the West — a byword for a trickster who can take any form. (Allusion.)

The famous saying Shaw is said to have ‘garbled’ is the old epigram that one who is not a radical in youth has no heart, but one still radical in age has no head — commonly credited to Guizot or Clemenceau, and, in an 1872 form, to the jurist Anselme Batbie citing Burke; Ye Qinian’s giving it to ‘a judge’ fits the Batbie strand. Its author is genuinely disputed. (The saying is corroborated; the attribution is not settled.)

ch13.anchor: there's a crab on your belly
ch13.note: The band is playing a foreign dance tune the novel calls ‘I Belong to Your Heart,’ which Chinese ears are said to have misheard as 肚皮上有一只蟹, ‘there’s a crab on your belly.’ The homophonic joke has the flavor of old-Shanghai lore, but it is untraceable in the reliable record, and no dance tune of exactly that title fixes it to 1933; treat it as a likely apocryphal grace-note. (Uncorroborated.)

Mr. Lifu is Chen Lifu (陈立夫, 1900–2001), who with his brother Chen Guofu led the Kuomintang’s ‘CC Clique’; as head of the Central Organization Department he stood over the Party Affairs Investigation Section, the KMT’s political-intelligence organ, and was in 1933 the controlling figure of its secret work — hence the man for Ye Qinian to ‘put in a word’ with. (Corroborated.)

Bogu — Bo Gu — was the alias of Qin Bangxian (秦邦宪, 1907–1946), de facto head of the Chinese Communists’ Provisional Central in Shanghai. Ye Qinian’s inference is historically exact: on a decision of 13 January 1933 the Provisional Central quit the dangerous Shanghai underground for the Central Soviet, and Bo Gu and his colleagues reached Ruijin by late January 1933 — just as a Red China article signed ‘Bogu’ would suggest. (Corroborated.)

ch14.note: The workers’ pickets (工人纠察队) were the armed labor militia of the Communist-led Shanghai workers’ uprisings that seized the Chinese city as the Northern Expedition neared in early 1927, above all the third uprising of 21 March 1927. Cui Wentai’s rise through the strikes and the pickets, and his shelter by Old Fang, set his whole history against these events. (Corroborated.)

The Twenty-Sixth Army (二十六军) of the National Revolutionary Army, under Zhou Fengqi and the overall command of Bai Chongxi, carried out the Shanghai side of Chiang Kai-shek’s April Twelfth coup of 1927: on 12–13 April it tricked the workers’ pickets into surrendering their arms and then machine-gunned the protesting crowd on Baoshan Road, seizing and shooting the pickets’ leaders. The novel’s naming of the 26th Army is historically exact. (Corroborated.)

The great floods of the twentieth year of the Republic are the catastrophic Central China floods of 1931, among the deadliest disasters of the twentieth century, which spread famine and epidemic disease, cholera among them; death-toll estimates diverge sharply, from around 145,000 in Chinese sources to some 3.7–4 million in Western ones. (Corroborated; the toll is estimated within a wide range.)

The New Year’s Eve table is set with Shanghai home-style (本帮) classics: zaobodou (糟钵斗), assorted pork offal stewed in fermented-glutinous-rice sauce; oil-seared shrimp (油爆虾); yanduxian (腌笃鲜), a soup of salt pork and fresh pork simmered with bamboo shoots; and the five-kernel New Year cake (年糕), whose name puns on 年年高, ‘higher year after year.’ (Corroborated.)

ch15.note: The storming of the Soviet consulate in Guangzhou is real: on 13 December 1927, retaking the city from the Communist ‘Canton Commune,’ Nationalist and allied forces raided the Soviet consulate-general and shot five of its staff, along with Chinese employees, and Nationalist China broke off relations with the USSR soon after. Whether Long Dong really died there is the novel’s question, not history’s. (The raid and the killings are corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains
ch15.note: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (千里江山图) is a real painting, and the novel’s title: a blue-green landscape handscroll on silk, about 51.5 cm high and 11.9 meters long, painted in 1113 by Wang Ximeng (王希孟), a pupil of the Song emperor Huizong, at the age of eighteen. It is his only surviving work and one of the most celebrated of all Chinese paintings, held today in the Palace Museum, Beijing. Here its name is the underground’s passphrase, and the mission is named for it — a thousand li of courier line, and a thousand li of the rivers and mountains of China. (Corroborated.)

The August 7th Conference (八七会议), an emergency meeting of the Communist Party’s Central Committee held secretly at Hankou on 7 August 1927, met in the wreckage of the First United Front after Chiang Kai-shek’s April purge. It repudiated Chen Duxiu’s ‘right opportunism,’ set the general line of land revolution and armed resistance to the Nationalists, and raised Qu Qiubai to the leadership; it was here that Mao Zedong pressed the view that political power grows from the barrel of a gun. (Corroborated.)

Jianren (简任) was the second-highest of the four grades of the Nationalist civil service (特任, 简任, 荐任, 委任), just below the ministerial 特任 appointments. The point is that the head of the Party Affairs Investigation Section, though only a middling official on paper, wielded power far beyond his nominal rank. (Corroborated.)

The Party’s clandestine courier lines (交通线) from Shanghai to the base areas were real. From 1930 the Central Liaison Bureau opened lines out of Shanghai; the enduring one, the famous ‘Central Red Route,’ ran Shanghai–Hong Kong–Shantou–Dabu–Ruijin and carried documents, funds, supplies and more than two hundred cadres (Zhou Enlai among them) into the blockaded Central Soviet until the eve of the Long March in 1934. Standard Party histories count three main lines (the Yangtze, Northern and Southern); the novel’s ‘four’ is its own figure, perhaps counting a secondary branch. (The lines are corroborated; the count of four is the novel’s.)

The Canton–Hong Kong Strike (省港大罢工) was the great general strike and anti-British boycott of 1925–26, launched in solidarity with Shanghai’s May Thirtieth Movement and inflamed by the Shakee (Shaji) shooting of 23 June 1925, when Anglo-French troops fired on demonstrators in Guangzhou. Lasting some sixteen months and drawing on the order of a quarter-million strikers, it is often called the longest strike in labor history, and the Communists were deeply involved in it. (Corroborated.)

ch16.note: The marten-paw fur (诱爪仁) — sewn, the novel says, from the tiny strips of skin below a marten’s claws, so that one robe might cost hundreds of animals — dramatizes a real practice of Chinese furriery, in which a garment is pieced from small prime parts (back, legs, paws) of many pelts. But this particular ‘under-the-claw’ category, and its extravagant claims, are not attested outside the novel and look to be its own embellishment. (The pieced-fur practice is corroborated; this specific fur is uncorroborated.)

The ABC of Communism (共产主义ABC) is a real book: Nikolai Bukharin and Yevgeni Preobrazhensky’s popular 1919 exposition of the Bolshevik party program, widely read in Chinese translation as an introduction to Communism in the 1920s. Letters from Afar is Lenin’s 1917 work (see the note at the earlier chapter that quotes it). To Ye Qinian these are the books that ‘turned’ the young Chen Qianli. (Corroborated.)

ch16.anchor: Tianjin Road was the street of the banks
ch16.note: Tianjin Road (天津路), in the old International Settlement just north of Nanjing Road, was a real hub of banks and native banks — part of the northern money market — and is commonly remembered as one of Shanghai’s ‘bank streets.’ (Corroborated.)

A native bank (钱庄, qianzhuang) was a traditional Chinese private banking house, the indigenous forerunner of the modern bank: it began in money-changing and grew into deposits, loans and remittance, running on personal credit and native-place ties and issuing its own money orders. In Republican Shanghai the native banks worked alongside the foreign and modern Chinese banks; the novel’s distinction between the 钱庄 and the modern 银行 is exactly right. (Corroborated.)

‘Big yellow croakers’ (大黄鱼) was old-Shanghai slang for gold bars: a ten-tael bar was a ‘big yellow croaker,’ a one-tael bar a ‘little yellow croaker’ (小黄鱼), ten little to one big, the names taken from the gold color and the rough fish shape. A ten-tael bar ran to roughly 310–373 grams, depending on the tael standard in use. Cui Wentai’s ‘five big yellow croakers’ are the five gold bars. (Corroborated.)

Seward Road (熙华德路), in Hongkou, was a real Settlement street built in 1864 and named for an American consul; in the 1943 wholesale renaming of foreign-named streets it became Changzhi Road (长治路), which it remains. (Corroborated.)

The Wang Jinzhi murder case appears to be the novel’s invention: no documented Shanghai crime by that name could be found in the reference record. Its setting, though, is real. Taikoo (太古) is Butterfield & Swire, whose China Navigation Company, founded in 1872, ran passenger-and-cargo steamers on the Yangtze between Shanghai and Hankou; a ship’s chafang (茶房), here rendered ‘steward,’ was the attendant who waited on passengers, and a trusted head steward carrying valuables upriver is true to the trade. (The case is uncorroborated; the Taikoo steamer trade is corroborated.)

ch17.note: The Nationalist gendarmerie (宪兵, military police) were a real standing force with police powers, an ordinary presence in 1930s Shanghai; armored cars (铁甲车) were likewise real, some built at the Shanghai Arsenal in 1929–30 with mounted machine guns. A garrison unit lending one to the secret police for such an operation is plausible for the period. (Corroborated.)

ch17.anchor: the Ministry of Finance's public-bond business
ch17.note: The detail hints at the power behind the small bank. That a ‘Mr. Song’ (宋) should have an all-important elder brother, and the bank a share of the Ministry of Finance’s bond issues, invites the reader to think of the Soong (宋) family, whose T. V. Soong (宋子文) was the Nationalist finance minister of just these years (1928–1933); the novel leaves the connection unspoken. The real Zhonghui Bank was in fact the Green Gang boss Du Yuesheng’s (see the note on the bank). (T. V. Soong and the finance ministry are corroborated; the identification of ‘Mr. Song’ is the reader’s inference, not stated.)

The Nanshi police were real. Shanghai had three separate forces — the Settlement’s Municipal Police, the French Concession police, and a Chinese municipal force over the Chinese-administered districts, headquartered in Nanshi (the Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau, so named from 1930). That the car belongs to the Chinese-city police, and that there might be Communists inside it, turns on this jurisdictional patchwork; the exact station name is the novel’s. (Corroborated.)

The Three Principles of the People (三民主义) — Nationalism, Democracy (people’s rights) and the People’s Livelihood — were Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine, given definitive form in his 1924 Guangzhou lectures, and the official ideology of the Nationalist party and state. Ye Qinian’s creed, that Communism is to be beaten not by killing but by converting minds to the Three Principles, is exactly the regime’s official line. (Corroborated.)

Professor Tao of Central University is most likely Tao Xisheng (陶希圣, 1899–1988), who joined National Central University in Nanjing in 1931 and was known as a theorist of the Three Principles, and who later ghostwrote Chiang Kai-shek’s China’s Destiny (1943). But in the early 1930s Tao was chiefly a social historian, and had earlier belonged to an anti-Chiang faction; his hard anti-Communist role crystallized only later, so a specific 1933 anti-Communist primer by him is not documented. The recommendation reads as the novel projecting his later authority back onto this scene. (The professor is corroborated; the book is uncorroborated.)

ch18.note: The French Concession Municipal Council (公董局, Conseil d’administration municipale) governed Shanghai’s French Concession — a separate authority from the Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) that ran the International Settlement. Its writ ran only to the north bank of the Zhaojiabang; the creek’s south bank was Chinese-administered ground, which is why the firm’s coal yard there lay beyond the reach of the Concession police. (Corroborated.)

A clue that works only in the written script. The dying Old Fang scrawls a half-formed 山 (shan, ‘mountain’); the traitor’s surname, Cui (崔), is written with exactly that element, 山, set atop the graph. The unfinished character therefore points to Cui Wentai. English can report the stroke but not the naming, which is why it needs a note.

ch18.anchor: the bone of a rebel in his skull
ch18.note: Wei Dafu reads Cui Wentai’s face by the old art of physiognomy. To have ‘cheekbones you can see from behind’ (脑后见萶) marked a man as treacherous and ungrateful; the bone of a rebel (反骨, literally a ‘bone of rebellion’) alludes to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which Zhuge Liang, spying such a bone at the back of the general Wei Yan’s skull, foretells that he will one day turn traitor. (A real physiognomic tradition and a real literary allusion; the reading of Cui’s face is the novel’s.)

ch18.anchor: the counter-revolutionary governments of Ninghan and Ningyue
ch18.note: Lin Shi compresses several years of Nationalist consolidation. The Ninghan (宁汉) split was the 1927 rupture between Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing (宁) government and the Wuhan (汉) government under Wang Jingwei; after Wang broke with the Communists the two reconciled, the Ninghan merger of September 1927. The Ningyue (宁粤) confrontation was the breakaway Canton (粤) government of 1931, later brought back into the fold. Chiang’s National Government then proclaimed the period of political tutelage (训政, October 1928): under Sun Yat-sen’s three-stage scheme — military government, tutelage, then constitutional rule — the Nationalist Party would wield power on the people’s behalf, in effect one-party rule as a transitional stage. (Corroborated.)

ch18.anchor: the thirteenth card in the deck
ch18.note: The operation’s code names are playing cards. Lin Shi’s, Laokai (老开), the text glosses as the King — the thirteenth card of a suit, ace through king. It is of a piece with the book’s running motif of games of chance: the dice of the opening chapters, the ‘game of chess’ the whole plan is likened to. (The novel’s device.)

ch19.note: February (二月) is a real novella by Rou Shi (柔石, pen name of Zhao Pingfu, 1902–1931), published by the Chunchao Book Company in Shanghai in November 1929 with a short preface by Lu Xun, who had edited it. Its hero, the schoolteacher Xiao Jianqiu, befriends a young widow whose husband was killed in battle and who is left with two small children — the book Ling Wen describes. Rou Shi belonged to the League of Left-Wing Writers and was one of its Five Martyrs, secretly shot by the Nationalists at Longhua on 7 February 1931 — the same killing ground, and all but the same month, that give this chapter and this novel their weight. Lu Xun’s memorial essay ‘In Memory of the Forgotten’ was written in February 1933, just when A Thousand Li is set. (Corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: the woodcut design was of the plainest
ch19.note: The novel makes the jacket a woodcut — a river bearing leaves, rain and human faces. The historical first edition of February in fact carried a line drawing by Tao Yuanqing (陶元庆, 1893–1929), among his last works, not a woodcut; the woodcut art Lu Xun championed came through his Morning Flower Society, not this cover. The image here is the novel’s own, and its drifting faces read as a quiet figure for the drowned dead the book commemorates. (The woodcut cover is uncorroborated; the design is the novel’s.)

ch19.anchor: a lawyer from the Relief Society
ch19.note: The Relief Society (济难会) was the China Relief Society, founded under Communist leadership in 1925 and reorganized as the China Red Aid Society (中国革命互济会) in 1929, the Chinese arm of the international Red Aid movement. It relieved the families of arrested and executed revolutionaries and, exactly as here, retained sympathetic lawyers to bail comrades out of prison. The Nationalist government banned it in 1934. (Corroborated.)

ch19.anchor: a cat curled at the stove
ch19.note: A cat curled at the stove renders weizaomao (牢灼猫), a Wu-dialect phrase — a cat drowsing at the kitchen fire — for a listless, spiritless creature. Wei Dafu resents the label; Chen Qianli turns it into praise a moment later, when at the crucial hour ‘the stove-cat turns into a tiger.’ (An idiom of the Shanghai region.)

ch20.note: Dashatou Station (大沙头站), built in 1911, was the Guangzhou terminus of the Canton–Kowloon Railway (广九铁路), the line to Hong Kong, and the city’s eastern railhead in this era; it was renamed Guangzhou East Station in 1947. Arriving from Hong Kong, Ling Wen and Yi Junnian would indeed have come in here. (Corroborated.)

ch20.anchor: Comrade Deng Zhongxia had lectured there
ch20.note: Deng Zhongxia (邓中夏, 1894–1933) was a founding leader of the Chinese labor movement and, with Su Zhaozheng, a chief organizer of the Canton–Hong Kong Strike; the strike committee ran worker-education bodies, a Labour College (劳动学院) among them, at which he lectured. He was arrested in Shanghai and executed by the Nationalists at Yuhuatai, Nanjing, in September 1933, months after this novel’s events. (Deng and the Labour College are corroborated; siting the college on the fourth floor of the Nanhua Building is the novel’s detail, unconfirmed in the record.)

ch20.anchor: Under Chen Jitang's rule of Guangdong
ch20.note: Chen Jitang (陈济棉, 1890–1954), the militarist called the ‘King of the Southern Sky,’ governed Guangdong all but independently of Nanjing from about 1929 to 1936, so his rule in early 1933 is accurate. His regime pressed a conservative, Confucian-revival social order, down to dress codes for women, which bears out the novel’s picture of a place where a man and woman sharing one rickshaw would draw the eye. (Corroborated.)

ch20.anchor: the roof of the Sincere Company
ch20.note: The Sincere Company (先施公司) was the first modern department store founded and run by Chinese, opened in Hong Kong in 1900 by the returned overseas merchant Ma Ying-piu, with branches in Guangzhou (1912) and Shanghai (1917). Its stores were famous for their rooftop gardens and amusement parks, in Guangzhou as in Shanghai. (Corroborated.)

Shamian (沙面) is the small islet in the Pearl River carved into British and French concessions after 1859, where the foreign consulates stood. It was from Shamian, across the narrow Shakee Canal, that Anglo-French troops machine-gunned the marchers of 23 June 1925 — the killing Yi Junnian recalls, part of the Canton–Hong Kong Strike noted earlier. (Corroborated.)

Three features of old Guangzhou build this scene. The bamboo-tube house (竹筒屋) is a townhouse narrow at the street but very deep, its rooms strung front to back like the joints of a length of bamboo. The arcades (骑楼, qilou) of the main streets are shophouses whose upper floors overhang the pavement on columns to shelter it. The Manchu windows (满洲窗) upstairs are lattices set with panes of colored, etched glass, a signature of the houses of the Xiguan district. (All corroborated as real Lingnan forms.)

The People’s Palace (平民宫) was real: a shelter for the poor, with dormitories, a night school and a library, completed in Guangzhou in 1931 under Chen Jitang. Contemporary accounts trace its seed money to funds seized from smugglers rather than, as Mrs. Mo has it, to fines on opium boats — though Chen’s government did draw heavily on opium and gambling revenue, so her version is close in spirit. (The People’s Palace is corroborated; the opium-boat-fine funding is uncorroborated in that exact form.)

The hanging-bell flower (吊钟, Enkianthus quinqueflorus), whose bell-shaped blooms open at the Lunar New Year, is a traditional Cantonese New-Year flower, sold at Guangzhou’s New-Year flower market (行花街). Shuangmendi (双门底, today’s Beijing Road) was the historic site of that market, which is what Ling Wen’s couplet conjures. (Corroborated.)

The Hao cipher (豪密) was real: a code devised by Zhou Enlai and named for his underground alias Wu Hao (伍豪), used in the Party’s secret and wireless communications from the late 1920s. It was a code-book cipher, and is generally held never to have been broken by the enemy. The novel’s worry — that overuse, above all on matters the enemy already knows, could betray a pattern — is a sound cryptographic principle and Old Xiao’s own reasoning, not a recorded failure of the cipher. (The Hao cipher is corroborated; the vulnerability is the novel’s caution.)

ch20.anchor: the Red Army captured a high-powered set
ch20.note: The outline is historical. The Party’s first secret radio was built in Shanghai in 1929, and Shanghai’s contact with the southern base areas was at first relayed through a clandestine Hong Kong station. At the Battle of Longgang (December 1930, the first anti-‘encirclement’ campaign) the Red Army captured a radio and won over its operators, though only the receiver survived — the famous ‘half a radio’; a high-powered transmitter taken in the second campaign, in 1931, made direct Shanghai–Ruijin wireless contact possible. (Corroborated; the novel telescopes the two captures into one.)

Zhu Huiri (朱晋日) was a real figure, appointed director of the Guangzhou Municipal Public Security Bureau in October 1927 and a hand in suppressing the Communist Canton Uprising that December. Whether he still held the post in the early 1930s is not clearly documented, but the novel’s use of him as Guangzhou’s police chief rests on a real official in a real office. (Corroborated as a real person and police chief; his exact tenure here is uncertain.)

The Guangzhou Republican Daily (广州民国日报) was a real Nationalist newspaper, founded in 1923 and reckoned an early party organ of the reorganized Kuomintang; it was renamed the Zhongshan Daily in 1937. (Corroborated.)

Lu Zhongde (卢忠德), the comrade planted in the public-security bureau, and Secretary Ouyang Min (欧阳民) of the special committee belong to Mrs. Mo’s story and appear to be the novel’s invention; no such figures surface in the record of the Guangzhou underground. They serve to set Long Dong’s shadowy intelligence work within a plausibly wrecked network. (Fictional, as far as the record shows.)

ch21.note: Haoxian Road (豪贤路) is a real east–west street in Guangzhou, near the Xiaobei Gate. Its older name, written 濠弦街 (‘moat-bowstring’), is documented: a stretch of the Song-dynasty city moat (护城濠) ran here, and the straight street beside it was likened to the string of a bow. The homophone 豪贤 (‘noble worthy’) was later substituted to honor the Ming loyalist poet-general Li Suiqiu (黎遂球, 1602–1646), a native son. The lane and address the searchers seek within it — Tianguan Li and its Rear Street, No. 23 — are the novel’s own. (Street and etymology corroborated.)

Wong Tai Sin (黄大仙, the Daoist immortal Huang Daxian) and the drawing of numbered bamboo oracle-lots (求签), each keyed to a fortune-poem, are genuine; a Wong Tai Sin temple stood at Fangcun in Guangzhou. The verse the diviner recites, however, is the novel’s invention: the real lot no. 73 is rated ‘supremely auspicious’ and titled ‘the top scholar returns home in glory,’ a poem of triumph — the reverse of the melancholy lines given here. (Deity and practice corroborated; the quoted lot-73 poem is the author’s substitution.)

ch21.anchor: one general's fame is built on ten thousand rotting bones
ch21.note: The closing line of ‘The Year Jihai’ (己亥岁) by the late-Tang poet Cao Song (曹松): ‘凭君莫话封侯事，一将功成万骨枯’ — do not speak to me of winning a title of rank; one general’s success is built on ten thousand rotting bones. It is a proverbial indictment of glory bought with common lives. (Corroborated.)

A self-combed woman (自梳女, zishunü) had, in a formal ceremony, combed up her own hair to vow lifelong spinsterhood and independence — a custom that flourished in the silk-reeling districts of the Pearl River Delta, above all Shunde (顺德), in the late Qing and early Republic. When the silk trade collapsed in the 1930s many took work as domestic servants, the amahs (妈姐) of Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Singapore. Qigu is one such. (Corroborated.)
Fo sui (火水, ‘fire-water’) is the Cantonese word for kerosene; Ling Wen, from the north, does not know it until she sees the lamp lit — a small mark of how foreign Guangzhou is to the two travelers.

The tanglong door (趟栊门) is the traditional three-part front door of the Xiguan houses of Guangzhou, exactly as described: outermost a pair of waist-high swinging screen half-doors (the ‘foot-gate,’ 脚门); behind them the 趟栊 itself, a gate of thick round hardwood bars that slides sideways on rollers, like a movable ladder laid on its side; and innermost the solid main door. With only the sliding bars closed, air passes through the house while the doorway stays secure — indispensable in Guangzhou’s heat and damp. (Corroborated.)

The gables are wok-ear walls (镬耳墙 / 锅耳墙), the tall curved gable-ends, shaped like the two handle-lugs of a cast-iron wok, that crown the grander houses and ancestral halls of the Lingnan region — a mark of status and, it was said, a guard against fire. (Corroborated.)

ch21.anchor: the great iron bridge over the Pearl River
ch21.note: The Haizhu Bridge (海珠桥), Guangzhou’s first iron bridge across the Pearl River, was completed in February 1933 — so Qigu’s landmark places the memory in the novel’s own present, years after the raid she is asked about; her sense of time, like much else about her, wanders. (Bridge and date corroborated.)

ch21.anchor: the eastern neighbor who apes Xi Shi
ch21.note: The diviner’s unfinished couplet is thick with old allusion. Xizi (西子) is another name for Xi Shi, the beauty of Yue — the same name the enemy has given their planted agent. ‘The eastern neighbor who apes Xi Shi’ fuses two images: the ugly woman of the Zhuangzi who imitated Xi Shi’s frown and only made herself hideous (东施效颦, the byword for grotesque imitation), and the paragon ‘daughter of the eastern house’ of Song Yu’s rhapsody. The cut-off second line turns on 郭素, read here as 郭索 — the sidelong scrabbling of a crab, from Yang Xiong’s Canon of Supreme Mystery — so that the eastern neighbor’s aping of Xi Shi is set beside a crab’s clumsy mimicry: both are false imitations. The old man is, in effect, naming Yi Junnian to his face as a false Xi Shi, a fraud who apes what he is not — and pays for it. The verse is the novel’s own (see the note on the Wong Tai Sin lot), and its last line is left unfinished as the diviner is killed. (The allusions are real; the reading of 郭素 as 郭索, and the line’s full sense, are necessarily uncertain given the truncation.)

ch22.note: The Da Mei Wan Bao (大美晚报, the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury) was an American-owned, foreign-registered Shanghai evening paper; its Chinese-language edition began on 16 January 1933, which places the mission in the novel’s present. Its foreign registration is just what made it, like Shen Bao, a relatively safe place to plant a coded contact advertisement. (Corroborated.)

The singer, a female xiaosheng (女小生, a woman playing the young-male role, an established role-type in Cantonese opera), is performing Ke Tu Qiu Hen (客途秋恨, ‘Autumn Lament of a Traveler’), a celebrated Cantonese naamyam (南音) narrative-song. ‘I am of the Miu surname, styled Lianxian’ names its supposed author, the Qing literatus Miao Lianxian (缪莲仙); the later line she reaches, ‘like the men and women who fled Qin into the Peach Blossom source,’ invokes Tao Yuanming’s fable of a refuge sealed off from a chaotic world — an ironic backdrop to the manhunt about to begin. (The song and its lines are genuine, in the transcription variants normal to a sung text; the traditional attribution to Miao Lianxian is disputed.)

The pistol is an FN/Browning Model 1900, the Belgian semi-automatic designed by John Browning; because a small pistol was stamped on it, it was known in China as the gun-brand pistol (枪牌撸子 / 枪牌手枪). Old Xiao’s joke — that it ought by rights to be the ‘pistol-brand pistol-pistol’ — simply reads the nickname back literally. (Nickname and stamp corroborated.)

The Reflection Institute (反省院) was a real Nationalist prison for political detainees, chiefly captured Communists, run from about 1929; the flagship Capital Reflection Institute in Nanjing was established by statute in 1931. Its inmates underwent a curriculum meant to make them renounce communism (自新 / 转向), and turned Communists served as its ‘moral-instruction officers’ (训育员), exactly as here. (Corroborated.)

Liao Zhongkai (廖仲恺, 1877–1925), the leading KMT leftist, finance minister of the Guangzhou government and a champion of alliance with the Soviets and the Communists, was shot dead outside the party headquarters in Guangzhou on 20 August 1925. Investigators laid the crime to the KMT right wing; it remains famously unsolved. The assassination is real; the hint that the fictional Ye Qinian had a hand in it is the novel’s own invention. (Assassination corroborated; the tie to Ye Qinian fictional.)

Dai Jitao (戴季陶, 1891–1949), a close associate of Sun Yat-sen, became after Sun’s death in 1925 the foremost theorist of Nationalist anti-communism: his pamphlets of that year reread Sun’s Three Principles to exclude class struggle and deny the Communists any place in the party — the doctrine later called ‘Daiism.’ He inspired the anti-Communist Sun Yat-senism Society. (His writings and role corroborated; his organizing of the secret gatherings described here is the novel’s dramatization.)

ch22.anchor: Feng Yuxiang had not yet made a prisoner of Cao Kun
ch22.note: Teacher Ye’s prophecy is fixed by a run of real events of 1924 (Republic Year 13): the Nationalists and Communists formed their First United Front at the KMT’s First Congress that January; Sun Yat-sen issued a Northern Expedition manifesto in September; on 23 October the warlord Feng Yuxiang (冯玉祥) seized Beijing and put President Cao Kun (曹锟) under arrest; and on 13 November Sun set out north for reunification talks. Ye foresees the Nationalist–Communist war fully two years before the 1927 purge. (Chronology corroborated.)

ch23.note: Central Park (中央公园) is the real park at the heart of old Guangzhou, on the city’s central axis. The site had held government offices for centuries: a provincial censorate under the Yuan, a military commandery under the Ming, and under the Qing first the mansion of the Prince Who Pacifies the South (平南王府) — the fief of Shang Kexi (尚可喜, 1604–1676), one of the three feudatory princes whose revolt convulsed the south in 1673–1681 — and, after the revolt was crushed, the Guangdong governor’s office. Sun Yat-sen proposed making it a public park in 1918; it opened in 1921 as the First Municipal Park, free to all, and was renamed Central Park in 1926 (today the People’s Park, 人民公园). (Real; corroborated, save that the ‘Central Park’ name dates only from 1926.)

Kang Youwei (康有为, 1858–1927) was the Cantonese reform leader behind the abortive Hundred Days’ Reform of 1898, and afterward a long-exiled traveler who left a record of his Travels in Italy. He is said to have brought back several white-stone sphinx statues from Italy and set them in the park. (Real person; the donated Italian sphinxes are attested in local histories, though only in popular sources.) The sphinx returns a page later, stamped on the Garrick tin.
Three Castles (三炮台) was a genuine British cigarette, launched in 1878 by W. D. & H. O. Wills of Bristol, later a founding brand of Imperial Tobacco. (Real; corroborated.)

Garrick (茄力克), the cigarette that gives the chapter its name, was a real British brand made by Lambert & Butler of London (also of the Imperial Tobacco group); its tins carried a black sphinx device. The brand is the chapter’s thread: Yi Junnian was shown smoking Garrick when he first appeared (ch. 8), and Chen Qianli now begins to suspect that the murdered Guangzhou constable Lu Zhongde — who alone in the city smoked the brand — and the Shanghai agent Yi Junnian may be one and the same man. (Brand and sphinx real and corroborated; the detail that it was shipped from England and sold only at the Shamian foreign hongs at a silver dollar the tin is the novel’s period color, uncorroborated.)

Fantan (番摊) is a traditional Chinese gambling game: players bet on the remainder — one, two, three or four — left when a heap of small counters is divided out four at a time under the croupier’s rake. Long a staple of the Guangzhou gambling houses. (Real; corroborated.)

Two Lingnan customs of the Dragon Boat Festival (端午, Duanwu, the fifth day of the fifth lunar month). The noon-hour charm (午时符) is a paper talisman pasted on the door at the peak-yang noon of the day to ward off pestilence; and to ‘wash in the dragon-boat water’ (洗龙舟水) is to bathe, children especially, in the swollen festival-season river, held to bring health and drive off ill luck. (Both real Cantonese customs; corroborated.)

The Qunfangyan was a female troupe (女班): all-female Cantonese-opera companies were a real Guangzhou phenomenon from about 1919 (the novel’s troupe-name echoes the actual 群芳艳影), barred at first from the great theaters, the mixed-sex ban lifting only after 1933. A huadan (花旦) is the young female-role lead, the xiaosheng (小生) the young male role; baotou (包头, here ‘head-dresser lead’) is an old term for the female-role player, from the hair-wrapping of the part. (Real; corroborated.)

ch24.note: Ten Beauties Round King Xuan (十美绕宣王) is a traditional Cantonese opera; the excerpt Untying the Red Silk (背解红罗) is its best-known scene. A foreign court sends the Han king a knotted length of red silk with the threat that unless someone can undo it the realm will be reduced to a vassal state; the whole court fails, and the minister’s clever daughter Su Jinding (苏金定) unties it and is taken into the palace — the seed of the harem tragedy that follows. Little Phoenix’s untying of the courtiers’ riddle shadows, at a slant, Chen Qianli’s own errand. (Real repertoire; corroborated.)

Presenting a star performer with a solid-silver shield (银盾), along with flower baskets and congratulatory plaques, was a real fashion of Republican-era theater patronage (捧角), best attested in Beijing and Shanghai. (The custom is corroborated; that it spread from the north to Guangzhou in the early 1930s, the shield’s size scaling to the giver’s wealth, is the novel’s coloring on a real practice.)

The Whampoa Military Academy (黄埔军校), founded in 1924 on Changzhou Island up the Pearl River from Guangzhou, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army under the first Nationalist–Communist united front; Chiang Kai-shek was its commandant and Zhou Enlai headed its political department. (Real; corroborated.)

The rumor points to the real Zhongshan Warship Incident (中山舰事件) of 20 March 1926. When the gunboat Zhongshan was moved to Whampoa — said to be without authorization by its acting commander Li Zhilong, a Communist — and amid rumors of a plot to seize Chiang Kai-shek, Chiang declared martial law in Guangzhou, arrested Li, disarmed the strike pickets, and purged Communists from the army and the Whampoa Academy. It was a decisive step in his consolidation of power and a turn toward the 1927 anti-Communist purge; standard scholarship holds the alleged ‘Communist conspiracy’ to have been pretext rather than fact. The constable’s bomb-and-letter provocation here (the novel’s invention) is imagined as the spark of just such a manufactured incident. (The incident is real and corroborated; the specific provocation is fiction.)

ch24.anchor: The rouge is all used up
ch24.note: The rouge is all used up (胭脂用尽). Little Phoenix’s parting message keeps the diction of the stage: the spent rouge is at once the paint of her trade, the beauty and youth she has poured out in three years of waiting, and, unspoken, the exhaustion of all she had to give him. The line is left as she speaks it, unglossed within the text. (Rendering the image; the reading is the translator’s.)

ch25.note: Dianshan Lake (淀山湖) is the real lake on the Qingpu–Kunshan border west of Shanghai, the largest natural freshwater lake in the Shanghai region and a source of the Huangpu River; the water town of Zhujiajiao stands on its shore. (Real; corroborated.)

ch25.anchor: fled all the way to Jiaoli
ch25.note: Jiaoli (角里), the chapter’s title, is the colloquial local name for Zhujiajiao (朱家角), the Ming-era canal town in Qingpu on the edge of Dianshan Lake, whose formal name was Zhuli (珠里). (Real and corroborated; here read Jiǎolǐ, and not to be confused with the archaic 甪里 / Lùlǐ near Suzhou.) The name suits You Tianxiao, who likes to parade a local’s knowledge of everything.

Shangta (商榻) is a real old town on the west side of Dianshan Lake in Qingpu. The etymology the novel gives is the attested one: it lay midway on the two-day water route between Suzhou and Songjiang, where trading boats put up (下榻) for the night — hence ‘where merchants lodge.’ (Real; corroborated.)

Songze (崧泽) is a real village in Qingpu, the type-site of the Neolithic Songze culture (c. 3900–3300 BCE), transitional between the Majiabang and Liangzhu cultures of the lower Yangtze. The novel carves the name on its roadside stone as 菘泽 (with the ‘cabbage’ radical), a folk miswriting of the standard 崧 — a fitting touch for the rustic byway Cui Wentai has blundered into. (Real; corroborated. The 菘 spelling is non-standard.)

Cui Wentai’s flight runs out along the real extra-settlement roads of western Shanghai: Brenan Road (白利南路, today Changning Road), Warren Road (华伦路, today Gubei Road) and Rubicon Road (罗别根路, today Hami Road), onto Hongqiao Road (虹桥路, still so named) and up to the Hongqiao airfield — the real Hongqiao Aerodrome, laid out from 1921 and in service as Shanghai’s air station from 1929. The line is a geographically coherent run west out of the city. (All real; corroborated.)

The Zhu-Hu county road (珠沪县道) — ‘Zhu’ for Zhujiajiao, ‘Hu’ for Shanghai — is the road being built to link the Qingpu county seat to the Hongqiao airfield. Qingpu did plan such a Zhujiajiao–Shanghai highway in 1932; for want of funds only the stretch to Hongqiao was built, opening in 1935–36, so in early 1933 it would indeed have been the raw, half-made dirt track the novel describes. (Real project; corroborated.)

Straw-tied pork (稻草扎肉) is a real Jiangnan dish and a noted specialty of Qingpu, of Zhujiajiao and Shangta above all: blocks of pork belly bound with rice-straw and red-braised, the straw both holding the meat and lending it its scent. (Real; corroborated.)

ch26.anchor: the school had been closed down by the Duan Qirui government
ch26.note: The Beijing Women’s Normal University (北京女子师范大学) and its suppression are real. During the student unrest of 1924–1925 against the headmistress Yang Yinyu, the education minister Zhang Shizhao, acting under Duan Qirui’s Beijing government, ordered the school dissolved and its students driven out by police in August 1925; Lu Xun, who taught there, took the students’ side in print and lost his ministry post for it. The school was restored the following year. Ye Tao’s return to Shanghai “that summer” matches the August 1925 closure. (Real; corroborated—the dissolution order issued from the minister Zhang Shizhao under Duan’s government.)

Zhaofeng Garden (兆丰花园) is Jessfield Park, the real public park in Shanghai’s western district (today Zhongshan Park in Changning). Laid out around the private garden of the English land-agent Hogg—whose firm gave it the name Jessfield—it was opened by the International Settlement’s Municipal Council in 1914 and kept that name until its wartime renaming in the 1940s, so “Zhaofeng Garden” is right for the period. It had an ornamental lake from the first; the pair of swans is the novel’s own touch, not a documented feature. (Real park; the swans uncorroborated.)

The books in this passage chart Ye Tao’s turn from anarchism and romance toward the new radicalism. The Captain’s Daughter is Pushkin’s 1836 novel of the Pugachev rising, among the first Russian works read in China; An Appeal to the Young (告少年) is Kropotkin’s famous anarchist tract of 1880, a formative text for a generation of Chinese youth; and New Youth (新青年, La Jeunesse), the magazine Chen Duxiu founded in 1915, was the organ of the New Culture Movement that swung, after 1919, toward Marxism. That she has left Kropotkin for New Youth as she leaves Esperanto for Russian marks the same drift. (All real; corroborated.)

Bakunin—Mikhail Bakunin (1814–1876), the Russian theorist of anarchism, whose quarrel with Marx split the First International—stands here for the anarchist creed of Ye Qinian’s salon; Ye Tao’s reply that it was Lenin who “had the right of it” marks her own passage from anarchism to Marxism–Leninism, the classic rupture of the age. (Real figures; the opposition historically apt.)

The three titles she sends are Marxist: The Communist Manifesto, whose first full Chinese translation, by Chen Wangdao, appeared in 1920; Letters from Afar (远方来信), Lenin’s five letters written from Zurich in March 1917 on the eve of his return to Russia; and The Bolshevik (布尔塞维克), the Chinese Communist Party’s central theoretical journal, published from 1927 to 1932 as successor to The Guide Weekly. (All real; corroborated.)

Plum Blossom Hill (梅花山) is a real rise on Purple Mountain outside Nanjing, set over the ancient tomb-mound of Sun Quan, founder of the kingdom of Wu; after Sun Yat-sen’s burial nearby in 1929 the hill was planted with plums and became the city’s great plum-viewing ground—so in the early spring of 1933 the plantings would still have been young. (Real; corroborated.)

ch27.anchor: the right-wing faction within the Nationalist Party
ch27.note: The backdrop is real. Under the First United Front (1924–1927) Communists served inside the Kuomintang; against it an organized anti-Communist right arose early, above all the Western Hills faction, which met near Beijing late in 1925 to demand the Communists’ expulsion. Ye Qinian’s cry that the Communists be “torn up root and branch” places the novel’s villain among that real right wing; the man and his speech are the author’s invention, the setting historical. (Backdrop real and corroborated; the character fictional.)

The Gonghexiang Wharf (公和祥码头), the chapter’s title, was a real dock on the Huangpu at the North Bund in Hongkou, run by the Gonghexiang wharf-and-godown company; on the old harbor maps it lay between the Shuntai and the China Merchants wharves. The site kept its wharf use for well over a century (later the Gaoyang Road wharf) and stands today within Shanghai’s international cruise terminal. (Real; corroborated.)

East Broadway (东百老汇路, today East Daming Road) is the real road running behind the Hongkou wharves; Americans of the settlement named it Broadway in 1877, after New York’s. The firms strung along it here were all real: the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company; the Wayside Wharf (汇山码头, “Wayside” rendered as 汇山), bought in 1903 by the Japan Mail Steamship Company (日本邮船会社, the N.Y.K. line); the Yehsong Dockyard (耶松船厂, S. C. Farnham’s British shipyard, later merged into the English United Dock Company); and the Shuntai Wharf (顺泰码头), a Jardine Matheson dock. (All real; corroborated.)

Borscht renders 罗宋汤, literally “Russian soup,” 罗宋 being an old Shanghai transliteration of “Russian.” The dish—and the fried pork chop served with it—came with the White Russians who fled to Shanghai after 1917 and opened its first Western restaurants; short of beetroot, local cooks rebuilt the soup on tomato, and it became a staple of the city’s home-grown Western cooking. (Real; corroborated.)

Leng (靓) is the common Cantonese word for “pretty, good-looking” (as in 靓女, a pretty girl); the colloquial reading leng is peculiar to Cantonese. The slip into it sets Lu Zhongde’s whole account in the Cantonese speech of Guangzhou. (Cantonese usage; corroborated.)

ch28.note: An allusion to Shanghai’s long conflict over 越界筑路, “extra-settlement road building”: from the 1860s the International Settlement’s Municipal Council laid and policed roads beyond its legal boundary into Chinese-administered territory (华界), in effect annexing the corridors. Boundary Road (界路, today’s East Tianmu Road) was the literal dividing line by the North Railway Station. The Lai’an Li case — a Cantonese company’s 1921 attempt to pull up the boundary stones and build across the line at the east end of East Xinmin Road, beaten back after protests by Zhabei’s civic bodies — is the real dispute the novel names. (Real; corroborated.)

ch28.anchor: To resist the foreign, one must first pacify the domestic
ch28.note: Ye Qinian is intoning the real Nationalist policy slogan 攘外必先安内 (rangwai bi xian annei), “to resist the foreign, one must first pacify the domestic.” Chiang Kai-shek advanced it from 1931 — most explicitly in an address of 30 November 1931 — to justify crushing the Communists and unifying the country before confronting Japan, which had just seized Manchuria in the Mukden Incident of that September. It is the governing policy of the years the novel depicts. (Real; corroborated.)

Huangniqiang (黄泥墙, “yellow-clay wall”) was a real locality in the western part of Shanghai’s old walled city, famous in the Xianfeng reign (1851–1861) for its honey-peaches (水蜜桃): an orchard of some three hundred trees there bore large, red-flushed, intensely sweet fruit celebrated across the city, until the trees were felled for housing as land values rose. The fame Ye Qinian recalls is genuine. (Real; corroborated.)

Zhuangyuanlou (状元楼) was a common name for Ningbo-style restaurants in Shanghai, where Ningbo cooking flourished after the port opened; the Ningbo sweet-rice dumplings (宁波汤团) ordered here, filled with black sesame and lard, are one of its emblematic dishes. The best-known Zhuangyuanlou, however, is usually dated to 1938, a few years after this scene, so a house of that exact name at Baxianqiao in 1933 is plausible in kind but not firmly attested. (The cuisine real; the specific restaurant uncorroborated for the date.)

The walled garden Xiaotaoyuan (小桃源, “Little Peach Spring”) — its name echoing Tao Yuanming’s idyll of the Peach Blossom Spring, a hidden refuge from the world — is the novel’s invention, though it is stocked, the text says, with peach trees transplanted from the real Huangniqiang. No such half-mu garden with a single walled door is attested in the old city. (Fictional; the peach-locality it draws on is real.)

A soldiers’ shelter-vault (藏兵洞) is one of the dead-end brick arch-chambers built into the Ming city wall and its barbicans at Nanjing, where troops sheltered and stores were kept in wartime. Those at the Shence Gate (神策门, the gate glossed at the Xuanwu Lake chapter) — the best-preserved of the wall’s Ming gates, on its northern stretch — are real; it is in one of them that Ye Tao’s body is found. (Real; corroborated.)

The Third Party was the 中国国民党临时行动委员会 (Provisional Action Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang), a left-Nationalist opposition founded in Shanghai in August 1930 under Deng Yanda (邓演达, 1895–1931) — set against both Chiang’s dictatorship and the Communists, and the forerunner of today’s Chinese Peasants’ and Workers’ Democratic Party. Deng was arrested by Chiang’s agents in 1931 and secretly executed at Nanjing that November. Ye Qinian’s claim to have “pulled Old Meng out” of it marks Old Meng as a real-world dissident. (Real; corroborated.)

ch28.anchor: Heaven and earth are not benevolent
ch28.note: Ye Qinian quotes the opening of chapter 5 of the Dao De Jing: “Heaven and earth are not benevolent; they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs” (天地不仁，以万物为刍狗). The straw dogs (刍狗) were figures plaited from straw for sacrifice, honored during the rite and thrown away once it ended; Laozi’s image is not of cruelty but of impartiality — nature acting by its own law, without favor. Ye Qinian twists it into a creed of the strong. (Real; corroborated as a classical source.)

ch29.note: The National Products Market (国货市场) belongs to the 国货运动, the National Products Movement — the patriotic campaign, strong through the 1920s–1930s and sharpened by anti-Japanese boycotts, to buy Chinese-made goods over foreign imports. Such markets gathered domestic manufactures under one roof. (Real; corroborated.)

ch29.anchor: only first class and third class
ch29.note: The foreign-run tram is the French Concession’s line, worked by the Compagnie Française de Tramways et d’Éclairage Électriques (法商电车公司), which ran the concession’s trams from 1908. The company is real; the narrator’s pointed detail that its cars had a first and a third class but no second — a graded slight to Chinese passengers — is the novel’s characterization, and is not confirmed by the tram histories consulted, which describe the early cars as first and second class. (Company real; the class detail uncorroborated.)

ch30.note: The Uchiyama Bookstore (内山书店) was a real Hongkou institution, opened by the Japanese bookseller Uchiyama Kanzō (内山完造) in 1917 and moved in 1929 to the foot of Scott Road; it held the city’s largest stock of Japanese books and quietly sold left-wing and banned titles. Lu Xun, a near-daily visitor from 1927 until his death in 1936, used it as a haunt and a meeting place. (Real; corroborated.)

ch30.anchor: the English sound of the cherry blossom
ch30.note: Chiai-li (千爱里) is a real lane of Japanese houses on Scott Road (today Shanyin Road) in Hongkou, the same block as the Uchiyama Bookstore, where Uchiyama himself lived. Chinese sources gloss its name as a “cherry-blossom residence,” after the Japanese for the sakura; the novel’s claim that it comes from “the English sound of the cherry blossom” is a folk etymology, not documented. (The lane and its cherry-blossom association real; the English derivation uncorroborated.)

The play names a real scandal. Ma Zhenhua was a young Shanghai woman who drowned herself in the Huangpu on 17 March 1928 after her fiancé publicly impugned her chastity and broke the engagement; the case filled the city’s newspapers and was dramatized on stage and screen as 《马振华哀史》 (“The Sorrowful History of Ma Zhenhua”). A scene of the wronged heroine writing a last letter before drowning fits those adaptations. (Real; corroborated.)

Football was a passion of the International Settlement, whose foreign-run association (西联会) ran a long-established First Division. Chinese sides competed at the top level, among them the team of Jinan University (暨南大学), a state university with a special mission to overseas Chinese; here it leads a foreign-merchant club, the “Lux” eleven. The named trophy (the Scotto Cup) and club are plausible period detail but could not be separately verified. (The league and Jinan real; the named cup and club uncorroborated.)

The Zhengjia wooden bridge (郑家木桥) was a real crossing over the Yangjingbang, the creek that divided the French Concession from the International Settlement; the creek was filled in 1914 but the name endured, long a byword for a disorderly quarter of pickpockets and hustlers along the concession line. (Real; corroborated.)

The Lantern Festival (元宵节) falls on the fifteenth of the first lunar month and closes the New-Year season — here, the day after this scene. Its foods run to sweet glutinous-rice balls and, as on Master Dong’s altar, eight-treasure rice and date cake. (Real; corroborated.)

Hart Road (赫德路, today’s Changde Road) was named by the Settlement authorities after Sir Robert Hart (1835–1911), the Ulster-born Inspector-General who ran China’s Maritime Customs for nearly half a century. (Real; corroborated.)

Standard gold (标金) meant the standardized gold bars traded — spot and as futures on margin — on Shanghai’s bullion exchange in the Republican era. To “fail at standard-gold speculation” was to be ruined betting on their price, a common road to bankruptcy in 1930s Shanghai finance. (Real; corroborated.)

The Three Heads (三头) are a celebrated set of Yangzhou (Huaiyang) dishes, exemplars of the cuisine’s fine knife-work and long braising: braised whole pig’s head (扒烧整猪头), stewed silver-carp head (拆烩鲢鱼头), and crab-roe “lion’s head” pork meatballs (蟹粉狮子头, here made with fish in the crab’s absence). The dishes are real and famous; the Yangzhou South Gate catering guild named in the chapter is plausible but not separately attested. (The dishes real and corroborated.)
